question: What is the main goal of epidemiology in public health?

options.B: Managing financial budgets for health clinics
options.C: Treating individual patients in a hospital ward
options.D: Studying how and why diseases spread in a population

explanation: Epidemiology is all about looking at the big picture—how and why health issues affect entire populations, rather than just treating one patient at a time. Great job wrapping your head around this community health fundamental!

question: Why do community health nurses need to know basic epidemiological terms?

options.A: To diagnose rare surgical conditions in the emergency room
options.B: To track illnesses and plan local health outreaches effectively
options.C: To calculate hospital building construction costs
options.D: To prescribe complex medications without consulting doctors

explanation: Spotting disease trends helps you plan amazing, targeted health outreaches for your community. You're building skills that save real lives!

question: In public health, what does 'incidence' specifically measure?

options.A: The number of recovered patients discharged from a ward
options.B: The percentage of patients who die from a specific infection
options.C: The total number of people living with a chronic illness
options.D: The number of new cases of a disease over a specific period

explanation: Think of incidence as the brand-new cases popping up during a set time frame. You've got this!

question: A village starts the year with no cholera, but 10 people fall sick by March. What do these 10 new cases represent?

options.A: The recovery rate of the infected population
options.B: The prevalence of cholera in the village
options.C: The mortality rate of the disease outbreak
options.D: The incidence of cholera for that period

explanation: Because these 10 folks developed the illness during that time window, they are the brand-new cases—making it the incidence!

question: How is 'prevalence' different from 'incidence'?

options.A: Prevalence only counts patients who are currently hospitalized
options.B: Prevalence includes all existing cases, both old and new
options.C: Prevalence is only used for vaccine trial evaluations
options.D: Prevalence measures how fast a disease spreads in a week

explanation: While incidence is just the *new* cases, prevalence is the grand total of everyone currently living with the condition (old and new together). Easy peasy!

question: Which measure should a clinic use when planning long-term care resources for people living with HIV?
explanation: To know how many resources (like drugs and counseling space) are needed overall, you need prevalence—the total count of everyone living with the condition right now.

question: When calculating an incidence rate, what goes into the denominator (the bottom number)?

options.A: The total number of deaths recorded in the hospital
options.B: The total budget allocated for public health programs
options.C: The number of patients who have already recovered
options.D: The total population at risk of getting the disease

explanation: When calculating rates, your denominator must only include people who can actually catch the disease. Makes complete sense when you think about it!

question: Why must people who already have a disease be left out of the denominator when calculating incidence?

options.A: They are usually transferred to a different clinic
options.B: They cannot develop a condition they already have
options.C: They skew the financial data of the health facility
options.D: They automatically increase the recovery rate statistics

explanation: Incidence tracks *new* infections. If someone already has the illness, they aren't at risk of catching it for the first time anymore!

question: What is another common name for incidence density?
explanation: Incidence density is also known as person-time incidence because it tracks the actual time units each person contributes to the study. You're mastering the terminology!

question: When is incidence density preferred over regular cumulative incidence?

options.A: When every single patient is followed for the exact same number of years
options.B: When the researcher wants to measure total existing chronic cases
options.C: When the population size remains completely frozen with zero movement
options.D: When participants enter a study at different times or drop out early

explanation: Real life is messy—people join studies late or drop out. Incidence density handles these rolling timelines like a champ.

question: What does a sudden spike in the incidence of a disease usually mean?

options.A: A potential disease outbreak starting in the community
options.B: An error in the hospital electronic record system
options.C: A successful completion of all vaccination programs
options.D: A decrease in the total population living in the area

explanation: A sudden jump in new cases is the classic red flag that an outbreak is kicking off. Spotting this early is a nurse's superpower!

question: How can public health nurses use incidence data to check if an immunization campaign worked?

options.A: By calculating the average age of patients in the ward
options.B: By measuring the total money spent on medical supplies
options.C: By checking if the number of new infections drops over time
options.D: By counting the total number of hospital beds available

explanation: If a vaccination drive is successful, you should see the number of new infections (incidence) go way down. Awesome nursing logic!

question: Which Nigerian agency relies heavily on routine disease reports and tracking to manage outbreaks?

options.A: Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency
options.B: Federal Ministry of Works and Housing
options.C: National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control

explanation: The NCDC is our national frontline defense, coordinating outbreak responses using data sent up from local health facilities.

question: A rural clinic notices a weekly increase in watery diarrhea during the rainy season. What should the nurses do first?

options.A: Ignore the data unless every single bed in the clinic is full
options.B: Close the clinic temporarily until the rainy season finishes
options.C: Wait until the end of the year to calculate annual averages
options.D: Report the trend upward to trigger quick public health support

explanation: Early reporting lets health authorities investigate water sources and rush supplies before things spiral into a full epidemic. You are thinking like a true public health nurse!
